Would she rather I worked some dead-end job for years like her? She was ridiculous. I knew I shouldn’t have visited her. It always ended in some kind of argument.

Being in the hospital always calmed down, and besides, I was on call, so I was sure I’d end up there at some point that night. Luckily, my mom lived close to the hospital, so I didn’t have a long drive. Despite the short distance, I found myself thinking about our fight.

paragraphs.body: As I pulled into the parking lot, I forced myself to stop thinking about it. It was only going to make me angrier. I walked into the hospital, heading for the on-call room, but I ran into my program director on the way there.
“Oh, nice to see you Dr. Graham. I was actually just about to call you,” he said.
“Nice to see you too, Dr. Miller. What did you want to talk about?” I asked.
“Maybe it’s better if we do this somewhere private.”
“Oh, right, HIPAA. Of course. I was just heading to an on-call room, if you wanted to talk there?”
“I think my office would be better for this, Dr. Graham.”

I couldn’t stop thinking about what case Dr. Miller wanted to discuss. Even though he was the residency director, he still took on patients of his own, and he always had fascinating cases. I was still daydreaming when we sat down at his desk.

paragraphs.body: “Dr. Graham, we looked into her chart. You prescribed blood thinners after her surgery,” Dr. Miller told me.
“I did. I wanted to prevent any clots from forming. I didn’t want to risk her having a heart attack or stroke,” I explained.

“You didn’t discuss this with one of your attendings beforehand. If you did, you would’ve realized that Ms. Smith had uncontrolled high blood pressure, and you would’ve been told not to prescribe blood thinners. Can you tell me why Ms. Smith wouldn’t have been given blood thinners, Dr. Graham?” he asked.

And I doubted they’d be able to deny me when they saw how good I was.

paragraphs.body: I thought back to my mom’s warning. She was right, I was close to the sun, but only because I was the best of the best. And maybe it was a long way down, but I would never know what the fall felt like.

annotations.comment: Waylon, you have this fascinating situation here, where a woman allllmost learns a lesson but then just doubles down on being a jerk. I wonder what happens to this story if she does actually learn the lesson — if this firing does actually break her — and then what happens? Maybe she goes back to her mom and apologizes? Maybe she tries to talk to the supervisor again? Or maybe she decides, nope, I did nothing wrong and I’ll apply elsewhere. (This is what you have now, except she never really changes or even seems like she might.) I do think you’ve at times gone beyond what makes logical sense — I couldn’t believe that a supervisor would fire his resident when she happened to wander into the hospital or that she could just apply elsewhere. So I would suggest thinking through that a bit, maybe trying to find someone’s online post about what happens when you get fired. I didn’t mind so much that I don’t much like Addie, but it was also hard to stay interested in her when she was a jerk to everyone. Is there anyone she’s nice to?Happy revising! Thanks!Grade: A
